## 6. Garage design

*Source: [garage-design.md](garage-design.md). The garage's visual UI style, persistent car upgrades, the current car stats display, and future scope for unlockable cars with different driving styles.*

The garage is where coins earned in runs buy permanent upgrades for the car. It is opened from the main menu. In the MVP it sells three upgrades, each with about 10 levels: acceleration, car HP, and a damage bonus for the car's weapons, shown as a plain list.

### Decisions

- The garage is opened from the main menu (how the menus connect: Game loop architecture, Decisions).
- The MVP garage sells three permanent upgrades: **acceleration** (reaching top speed faster), **car HP**, and a **damage bonus** in percent for the car's weapons.
- Each upgrade has about 10 levels. The Game Data Agent works out each level's price and how much it improves.
- In the MVP the garage screen is a plain list: each upgrade with its current level, the price of the next level and a button to buy it, plus the player's coins and a way back to the main menu. Its visual style comes after the MVP.
- The player's coins and the upgrade levels bought are saved to disk, so they are kept between game sessions.
- **Pickup magnet upgrade** (board, 2026-10-21): the radius within which coins, gift packs and health drops are pulled to the car (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Pickup magnet") is a garage upgrade, starting at 1 car length; its levels, prices and how far each level reaches are the Game Data Agent's proposals. Built in T-224 (proposal): 10 levels, radius 3.0 units (1 car length) at level 0, +0.6 units (a fifth of a car length) per level, 9.0 (3 car lengths) at level 10; prices 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 120, 155, 190, 240, 300, the same curve as the acceleration upgrade. The numbers live in `game/data/garage.json`. Its name and description in the garage: T-223. (T-224)
- **Air turn upgrade** (board, 2026-10-22): a fifth garage upgrade raises how fast the car spins in the air (Drifting, Decisions, "Slower air turn, upgradable"), from the new base of 1.25 times the ground rate. Its levels, prices and how much each level adds are the Game Data Agent's proposals (the Project Lead's suggestion: back up to today's 2.5 at the top level). Built in T-270 (proposal): 10 levels, the value is the air turn's total multiplier of the ground rate, 1.25 at level 0 and +0.125 per level, 2.5 (today's old value) at level 10 (1.375, 1.5, 1.625, 1.75, 1.875, 2.0, 2.125, 2.25, 2.375, 2.5); prices 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 120, 155, 190, 240, 300, the same curve as the acceleration and magnet upgrades. Reasons: an eighth of the ground rate per level is the old 2.5 split into ten even steps, so the top level gives back what T-269 took away; an air 360 off the tallest rooftop needs a total of about 1.9 (Drifting, T-269's notes), so it becomes reachable at level 6 (2.0, with a margin; level 5 gives 1.875, just short), and the air 180 is there from level 0; one shared price curve keeps the five upgrades comparable until the playtest. The run takes the bought level's value minus the base and passes it to the car's `apply_air_turn_bonus()` at every run's start (`CarTuning.apply_air_turn_upgrade`, called in `GameFlow.start_run()`); the drift prototype never gets it. The numbers live in `game/data/garage.json`. Its name and description: T-268. (T-270)
- **The car health upgrade adds hearts** (board, 2026-10-28): with hearts (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Hearts instead of health points"), each level of the car health upgrade adds 1 heart to the 5 the car starts with. Its description names no number, so it stays as it is. (T-333) Data: `car_health` in `game/data/garage.json`, unit `hearts`, base 5, +1 per level to 15 at level 10; the 10 levels and their prices (40 to 300) are unchanged, they still make sense.
- **Pixel art icons for the upgrades** (board, 2026-10-29): each garage upgrade gets a small pixel art icon, shown beside its row in the garage. One art ticket per upgrade (acceleration, car health, damage bonus, pickup magnet, air turn), each icon its own PNG in `game/art/garage/<upgrade key>.png`, which the garage picks up on its own; placeholders drawn in code until then. Script-drawn first (no PixelLab go yet), in the bold comic look of the HUD's reaction icons. (T-365, T-366 to T-370)
- **A broken save never wipes progress** (board, 2026-10-30, audit): a save file that fails to load is never overwritten; the game keeps a backup of the last good save and loads it. Each save records its version, so a renamed upgrade keeps its level. The same goes for the runs list. (T-417) Built as: a save is written to a temp file and renamed; the previous good file becomes `<file>.bak`; a file that fails to load is renamed to `<file>.broken-<time>` and kept; `version` starts at 1 (a file with none is 1), and a renamed upgrade id is mapped in `PlayerProgress.ID_RENAMES`.

### Content

#### Pickup magnet text (T-223)

The fourth upgrade's text, in the form of the other three (name up to 25 characters, description up to 80; T-224 uses it word for word, with the key `pickup_magnet`). It names no number, because the Game Data Agent proposes how far each level reaches.

| Key | Text | Length |
|---|---|---|
| garage.pickup_magnet.name | Brand Magnet | 12/25 |
| garage.pickup_magnet.desc | Coins and drops fly to you from further per level. | 50/80 |

#### Air turn text (T-268)

The fifth upgrade's text, in the form of the other four (name up to 25 characters, description up to 80; T-270 uses it word for word, with the key `air_turn`). It names no number, because the Game Data Agent proposes how much each level adds.

| Key | Text | Length |
|---|---|---|
| garage.air_turn.name | Spin Doctor | 11/25 |
| garage.air_turn.desc | Spin faster in the air per level. More flips, more views. | 57/80 |

#### Upgrade icons (T-365)

Each upgrade row begins with a small icon. The art is `game/art/garage/<upgrade key>.png` (a proposal: 16 x 16, drawn at 3x with hard pixel edges), one file per upgrade (`acceleration`, `car_health`, `damage_bonus`, `pickup_magnet`, `air_turn`); the art tickets T-366 to T-370 each add only their file and the garage picks it up with no code change. A missing file shows a grey pixel-square placeholder drawn in code, without text or Greenbull's colours. The rest of the row is unchanged. (Built in T-365: `game/docs/garage/garage-screen.md`.)

#### Saving

The player's coins and the level of each upgrade are kept in one small file under `user://` (`progress.json`), so they last between game sessions. A missing file means a new player: 0 coins, every upgrade at level 0. When a run ends, win or loss, the coins it collected are added to the total and saved. Buying an upgrade spends its price, raises its level by one and saves; it is refused, with nothing changed, when the player has too few coins or the upgrade is at its last level. The functions the garage screen and the run call are in `game/docs/data/game-data.md` ("Game data", "Saving and buying").

- **Keyboard** (board, 2026-11-02, T-492): the garage works with the arrow keys alone. It opens with the first upgrade's Buy selected; Up and Down (or W and S) walk the Buy buttons in the list's order, then Back, and wrap round (Left and Right, or A and D, keep the selection where it is; W, A, S and D work exactly like the arrows, board, 2026-11-02); Enter or Space presses the selected button; the selection shows with the shared button's focus plate. A Buy that is too expensive ("Not enough coins") can still be selected (it just does nothing); a fully funded upgrade's hidden Buy is skipped, and if it was selected the selection moves to the next one. Only fresh presses count, so a key held when the screen opens does nothing. The mouse works as before. How it is built: `GarageScreen.focus_order` and `KeyNav` (`game/scripts/ui/key_nav.gd`).

#### The garage screen (MVP)

A plain list (task T-058, `game/scenes/menu/garage_screen.tscn`, script `game/scripts/menu/garage_screen.gd`, `GarageScreen`). From the top: the heading, the player's coins, one row per upgrade, and a back button. Each row shows the upgrade's name and description, its current level, the price of the next level and a buy button. All text is the approved text from task T-059. Buying calls the save-and-buy object (`PlayerProgress`), and the whole screen redraws from it: the coins, the level and the price. When the player cannot afford the next level, the buy button is disabled and the row says "Not enough coins". At the last level the price and buy button go and the row says "Fully Funded". The back button only sends a signal; connecting it to the main menu, and the main menu's Garage button to this screen, is the screen flow's job.

#### How the garage fits the window (T-470)

The whole list (heading, coins, the five rows and Back) is one column, measured at its natural size (descriptions wrap in a 300 px width so a long one never widens a row) and scaled to the largest size that fits the window, then centred. Every Buy button and Back are therefore fully on screen at any window size: the base 1152 x 648, 1920 x 1080, ultrawide 2560 x 1080 and small windows (960 x 540). It refits whenever the window is resized. Like the HUD (T-431) the column uses nearest filtering and the scale follows the window, but it has no size slider.

### References

- The upgrade prices and effects: `game/data/garage.json` (task T-056).


## 7. Visual style

*Source: [visual-style.md](visual-style.md). The visual style for generated art (pixel art, isometric). May connect to the narrative theme.*

Solid Carbide is retro-feeling 2D pixel art in a 3/4 isometric view, set at night in downtown Tokyo under a kaiju attack. The city is steel and glass with small amber accents; the alien boulders and meteors glow navy, purple and magenta; the game's own effects glow pink and cyan; the sponsor Greenbull's colours, a leading dark green with light green and a little yellow, appear only on Greenbull's own things and on the car. The player drives a car in Greenbull's dark green, Mustang-inspired with white stripes, through cracked streets, chased by green lizard minions and a Godzilla-style kaiju. All art follows one technical style: hard-edged pixel art at 32 art pixels per unit, with a selective dark outline, detailed shading and a limited palette. The rules every asset is checked against are in Content, "Rules".

### Decisions

- The first map's city is cyberpunk and futuristic, in a Tokyo style, with skyscrapers and modern buildings.
- All roads are asphalt.
- Obstacles are drawn as boulders (in the MVP, crashed meteor boulders; Level design, Decisions).
- When the car drives behind a building, the building turns see-through so the car stays visible.
- How buildings turn see-through (from task T-020's research): the whole building fades while the car is behind it, to **15% visible**, over **0.15 seconds**, and fades back when the car comes out. Only buildings actually covering the car fade. In the MVP only the car is kept visible this way, not enemies or the kaiju; the board may revisit this after playtests.
- **Pixel-art technical style** (from the board's reference image, References): true pixel art drawn at its final size, never scaled up; hard pixel edges with no anti-aliasing and no semi-transparent pixels; transparent backgrounds; a dark, almost black **selective outline** (broken by lighter highlight pixels); **detailed shading**; **high detail**; a limited palette of about **30 colours per sprite**.
- **Scale:** **32 art pixels per unit** (1 unit = the car's width), drawn at scale 0.5 in the game, so the car is about 96 art pixels long. The car's frames are **128 by 128 pixels**. Everything else in the world (buildings, boulders, enemies, ground) is drawn at the same scale.
- **View:** a 3/4 isometric view, seeing the top and one side. The final car art is drawn for the isometric view only; the flat top-down view keeps the placeholder.
- **Palette:** a dark navy and purple night base, with pink and cyan neon accents. The sponsor's colours are not part of the city's palette; they appear only on Greenbull's own things (Greenbull's look, below).
- **Mood:** the game is set at night and should feel retro.
- **Glow:** drawn into the sprites themselves, as bright pixels with small, stepped halos of darker shades. No smooth blur or bloom effects from the engine, which keeps the retro pixel look.
- **Real-world references are inspiration only:** generated art never shows real brand logos or badges (for example no Ford or Shelby badges), and creatures are never exact copies of existing characters (the kaiju is Godzilla-style, not Godzilla).
- **The car:** inspired by a 1967 Ford Mustang GT fastback, in dark green as the main colour, with two parallel white racing stripes running down its length (bonnet, roof and boot), centred on the car as much as possible, with a gap of body colour between the two stripes. See the reference photos in References.
- **Buildings:** Tokyo-style towers with vertical signs and lit windows. The city has nothing to do with Greenbull, so the buildings carry none of its colours or branding. After the MVP, occasional Greenbull banners may be added as separate assets placed on the buildings, not drawn into them.
- **Buildings, redesigned** (board, 2026-10-14; replaces the dense narrow towers of earlier the same day): downtown Tokyo **under attack from the kaiju**. Each 30 by 30 block is split into **2 by 2 skyscrapers**, drawn as the bases of really tall towers whose tops are out of view, so the car is realistic in size next to them; **6 different skyscrapers**. **Shorter buildings** whose roofs show fill some of the slots. **Every building asset has a pavement drawn around it**, inside the block. **A few** alert banners about the kaiju hang on buildings or stand as signs on the pavement, with silly, minimalistic pixel paintings of its head or its Godzilla-like body. The signs may show Japanese-like marks that are not real words. All the city's art follows one brief from the Narrative Theme Agent (task T-128) so it stays consistent.
- **City brief** (board, 2026-10-15, from the Narrative Theme Agent's brief in task T-128; every city asset follows it): night; the city's colours are set by the "City colours" decision below; vertical neon signs with Japanese-like marks that are not real words, and no real brands; **pavements** a lighter, cooler grey than the asphalt, with a raised kerb on the road side and light cracks; **damage from the attack light to medium**: cracks, a few broken or dark windows, a little rubble, and no big fires, collapsed buildings or gore; the **alert banners are picture-only**, with no words, and look like road warning or prohibition signs: a red outline, a plain white inside, and only the black silhouette of the kaiju (its head or its Godzilla-like body shape), with no other detail and no neon colours (board, 2026-10-15; replaces the first cyan and pink drawings); the larger ones hang on buildings, small standing signs are on the pavement, and only a few on the map; kept out: Greenbull's colours, branding and bull logo, real brands, real words, the name Godzilla or an exact copy of the film monster, and any name for the kaiju.
- **City colours** (board, 2026-10-15, after playing the first skyscraper sample in the game): the city must **not share the boulders' palette**. The boulders and the kaiju's meteors are alien, so their navy, purple and magenta glow must stand apart from the city, never match it. The city is **less neon**: real concrete, glass and lit windows, with only small, muted signs. The board judged two palettes in the game, A (concrete and sodium light: warm greys and beige, yellow-orange windows) and B, and chose **B, steel and glass**: **cool blue-grey walls, pale white and pale blue lit windows, and small amber accents** (signs, shop lights) (board, 2026-10-15). Every city asset (skyscrapers, shorter buildings, pavements) uses the chosen palette; the alert signs keep their own warning-sign colours.
- **The rebrand: Redgull becomes Greenbull** (board, 2026-10-26): the sponsor is renamed **Greenbull**, one word, in a complete rebrand: a new name, logo and colours. It replaces Redgull, its seagull logo and its red everywhere. The old Redgull art stays in the archive (Every generated asset is kept).
- **Greenbull's look** (board, 2026-10-26): the logo is a **bull's head**, cool and bold, its own design: nothing like the real energy-drink logo of two charging bulls. It comes as an **emblem** (the head alone) and a **wordmark** (the head with the name GREENBULL in pixel letters). Its colours are **dark green, light green and yellow**, and the same three are the company's palette: **dark green is the main theme colour**, light green supports it, and **yellow is a small accent, used sparingly**. Proposed values (Project Lead, for the board's review): dark green RGB 12, 76, 44, the car's own body green, so the car already wears the sponsor's colour; light green RGB 104, 220, 96; yellow RGB 247, 208, 52. The logo is flat brand art, so it is exempt from the shading and detail of rule 2 (Content, "Rules"). The colours are used only on things that belong to Greenbull: its logo and wordmark, its banners (after the MVP) and, in the MVP, the weapons, which arrive as Greenbull gift packs, the helicopter that drops each gift pack, the package itself, which carries Greenbull's brand, and the level-up screen (the drop: Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Gift pack drop"). They don't have to be all green; the colours are included where they fit. The dark green is also the car's colour (The car), which is not changed. The emblem and wordmark are made through the style loop (`tasks/README.md`, "The style loop"). The game-ready files are in `game/art/logo/`: `greenbull_emblem_128.png`, `_64.png`, `_32.png` (T-294, run 2) and `greenbull_wordmark.png` (T-295, run 1), each with a json record beside it (T-300).
- **Red after the rebrand** (proposal for the board's review, 2026-10-26): with Redgull gone, red is no longer a brand colour, so it is no longer reserved. The reds already in the game stay as they are, each because of its subject: the kaiju alert signs' traffic-sign red outline (board, 2026-10-15), the car's pale tail lights (RGB 230, 110, 102; board, 2026-10-25), the minion's dull pink mouth (RGB 147, 93, 93; board, 2026-10-26), the health canister and the combo broken popup's warning red. The HUD's likes heart stays red, as a social-media heart.
- **Ground:** asphalt roads with **white** lane lines and **zebra crossings** at the junctions, with **light cracks** from the disaster; the centre is dusty gravel. No pavements in the MVP (after the MVP: Level design, Open questions).
- **Boulders:** dark rock with glowing cracks.
- **Challenge arrow** (after the MVP, if challenges come back; Level design, Decisions, 2026-10-11): a glowing painted arrow that draws itself along the path, pulses while the challenge is open, and fades when it is completed. Arrows of the challenges on the map are **blue**; arrows of the challenges the kaiju's meteors create are **green**.
- **See-through rule:** the no-semi-transparent-pixels rule covers the pixels inside each sprite. The game itself may fade a whole object, such as the kaiju's shield or a building the car drives behind.
- **Kaiju shield** (not in the MVP: the kaiju can be damaged at any time, Enemies, Decisions, 2026-10-11): while the kaiju can't be hurt, it is surrounded by a **green, see-through, oval shield**, the same green as its challenges' arrows. When one of those challenges is completed, the shield disappears and the kaiju shows its normal look while it can be hurt.
- **Effects** (gun bullets, exhaust flames, enemy hits and deaths, burning, coins, car damage, drift smoke and tire tracks, level-up; challenge completed after the MVP, if challenges come back): designed by the Asset Generation Agent within the palette, glow and pixel style above.
- **Level-up effect:** when the player levels up, the car gives off a burst of pixel-art particles. The particle sprites are drawn by a script, not generated with PixelLab, within the palette, glow and pixel style above, and not in Greenbull's colours. They pop out or shrink rather than fading. Approved look (T-074): six shapes (cyan and pink four-point stars, pink and cyan diamonds, a violet pixel cross, a small cyan spark), each with a white-hot core and darker halo pixels, one random shape per particle.
- **Drift marks:** while the car drifts, its two rear tyres leave dark tyre marks on the ground, which stay for a few seconds and then fade out as a whole. The mark texture is drawn by a script, not generated with PixelLab, within the pixel style above, and not in Greenbull's colours.
- **The neon underglow drawn in code** (board, 2026-10-22, after playtests): the board doesn't like the generated underglow sprite (T-175). The neon zone under the car is drawn in code instead, like the drift marks and the burning likes bar: pixel-art neon rings and glow made of bright pixels with stepped halos (no engine blur or bloom, per "Glow" above), in the underglow's purple and pink, never in Greenbull's colours, marking exactly its damage circle at every tier and following the car's height (Weapons, Decisions, "The underglow and the wiper at height"). The look (pulse, shimmer, rings) is the agent's proposal for the playtest. The T-175 sprite is kept, not deleted. (T-274)
- **Hype drift trail** (board, 2026-10-22): the drift marks change and gain effects with the hype level, on the combo heat steps (x2, x3, x4 and up; HUD and menus, Decisions), so a hotter combo leaves a hotter trail; below x2 they stay the plain tyre marks. The effects for each step are the agents' proposal for the playtest, drawn in code (no PixelLab), within the pixel style above and never in Greenbull's colours. Built (T-249, proposal for the playtest): x2 gets a yellow glow along the marks and a few yellow sparks off the tyres; x3 an orange glow that flickers, a yellow core line down the mark and more orange and yellow sparks; x4 and up a wider orange, light orange and yellow flickering glow, a white-hot core, many white, yellow and orange sparks, and flames rising off the tyres. A mark keeps the look of the step it was laid at. All opaque pixel squares and solid lines, no fading inside a sprite. (T-249)
- **Drift smoke:** while the car drifts, puffs of smoke come off its two rear tyres, stay where they were left, grow and then shrink or break up. The smoke sprites are drawn by a script, not generated with PixelLab, within the pixel style above (no semi-transparent pixels), and not in Greenbull's colours.
- **Every generated asset is kept, and kept apart by status.** Art that is clean and ready for the game lives under `game/art/`. Every other generation (rejected versions, failed attempts, test runs, edits the board didn't choose) is never deleted: it is archived, with its record, in `art-archive/` at the top of the repo, outside the game folder, one folder per task. So `game/art/` holds only assets fit for the game, and the archive holds everything else.

- **The HUD style sheet** (T-430, goal G-008 "A consistent HUD"; HUD and menus, Decisions, "A consistent HUD"; the values are a proposal for the board's playtest, the agents' reading of what the HUD already does most): every HUD piece (clock, coins, hearts, weapon icons, sub goal, live viewers counter and its fire, reactions, trick and combo broken popups, kaiju health bar, pause strip, level-up screen) follows these seven rules. The values live in `game/scripts/hud/hud_style.gd`; `game/tools/hud_sheet_check.py` checks the art.
  1. **Pixel scale:** HUD art is drawn at 1x and shown at an **integer scale, 2x** (one art pixel is two screen pixels), nearest filtering; text sizes are even numbers. Nothing is shown at a fraction (0.75x, 1.5x) or filtered.
  2. **Outline:** **1 art pixel (2 screen pixels) in (8, 8, 15)**, the near-black `HudStyle.OUTLINE_COLOR`, round every sprite and panel; a few lighter highlight pixels may break it (at most 15% of the edge, as everywhere in this game). Text and bars use the same colour: **text outline 6 screen pixels**, big numbers (the counters, the weapon count) 8, a bar's outline 2 screen pixels. Effects (the fire, glows) keep a dark red-brown edge instead, since they are light, not objects.
  3. **Palette:** the outline (8, 8, 15); a blue-grey steel bezel ramp lit from the top left for panels; screen black (10, 12, 17); white and light blue-grey (235, 242, 255) for labels; the viewers cyan (51, 225, 255) for everything about viewers; the heart red (219, 26, 41) for hearts only; pink (255, 72, 160) for effects and the subs badge; the warning red-orange (255, 80, 16) for crashes and the broken combo; the burning likes bar's yellows and oranges (255, 250, 209 / 255, 224, 77 / 255, 184, 41 / 255, 153, 20) for heat and fire; the coins' gold (255, 209, 64); neon purple (184, 46, 255) for the kaiju. Never Greenbull's light green or yellow (rule 6) outside its own things (the level-up screen and the gift pack).
  4. **Panels:** rectangles (and the one square, the sub goal), never round; a **stepped corner of radius 2** (pixels (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1) cut), a 3 pixel steel bezel lit from the top left with four screws on the clock and viewers panels, a black screen inside; the sub goal square keeps a white ring between two outlines in place of the bezel, since it must read over the street, and its black inside stays (4, 4) to (59, 59).
  5. **Font for words:** **Bangers** (`res://fonts/bangers/Bangers-Regular.ttf`), smoothing off, in capitals; every label, button and title in the HUD and its screens, with no system or default font.
  6. **Font for numbers:** the **clock's drawn seven-segment digits** (`clock_digits.png`, tinted by the game) for the clock; every other number (coins, subs, viewers, weapon counts, the popups' amounts) in Bangers, like the words. No monospaced system font (Consolas varies by computer).
  7. **Shading:** two or three steps of fill with the light from the top left, a white glint on round things, no gradients and no transparency inside a sprite (only 0 or 255 alpha).

  Checked in T-430: every HUD piece in `game/art/hud/` already fits except the sub goal frame, whose corners had radius 3 (redrawn by script with radius 2, `game/tools/build_hud_livestream_art.py subgoal-frame`, old version in `art-archive/T-430/before/`). What does not fit and is not art-by-script: the code's fonts and outlines, and the weapon icons, which are 64 x 64 pictures shown at 0.75x (rule 1): they need new 24 x 24 art (a PixelLab task, for the board). The piece-by-piece list is in T-430's result notes.

Other versions: `art-archive/T-465/`.
- **The splash cover** (board, 2026-10-29, an MVP nice-to-have): an AI-generated pixel art image behind the main menu, the game's cover for now. ### Content

#### Rules

The visual style guide: every generated or script-drawn asset is checked against these rules, each written once here (with Extended narrative's Text rules, the style guide the style loop scores against; `tasks/README.md`, "The style loop"). Each rule condenses the Decisions above; when a decision changes, its rule changes with it. Rules marked *(script)* are checked by a script, the others by the Style Evaluator.

1. **Pixel art** *(script)*: true pixel art drawn at its final size, never scaled up; hard pixel edges, no anti-aliasing; every pixel fully opaque or fully transparent; a transparent background; at most 30 colours per sprite. (Decisions, "Pixel-art technical style")
2. **Outline and shading:** a dark, almost black selective outline, broken by lighter highlight pixels; detailed shading; high detail. (Decisions, "Pixel-art technical style")
3. **Scale and view** *(script, size)*: 32 art pixels per unit (1 unit = the car's width), drawn at 0.5 in the game; the car's frames are 128 x 128; a 3/4 isometric view showing the top and one side. (Decisions, "Scale", "View")
4. **Night and retro:** every scene is at night and feels retro. (Decisions, "Mood")
5. **Glow is drawn, not rendered:** glow is bright pixels with small stepped halos of darker shades, inside the sprite; no smooth blur or bloom. (Decisions, "Glow")
6. **Greenbull's colours** *(script)*: the sponsor's palette is dark green RGB 12, 76, 44 (the main colour), light green RGB 104, 220, 96 and yellow RGB 247, 208, 52 (a small accent, used sparingly). The light green and the yellow appear only on Greenbull's own things: its logo and wordmark, the gift pack and its helicopter, the weapons and the level-up screen. Never on the enemies, the city, the ground, placeholders or code-drawn effects. The dark green leads on Greenbull's things and is also the car's body colour; it is never on the city or the ground. Red is not reserved (Decisions, "Red after the rebrand"). (Decisions, "The rebrand", "Greenbull's look", "Red after the rebrand")
7. **The city** (buildings, pavements, rooftops, ramps): steel and glass: cool blue-grey walls, pale white and pale blue lit windows, small amber accents, only small muted signs; never the boulders' navy, purple and magenta; light to medium damage (cracks, a few broken or dark windows, a little rubble), never big fires, collapsed buildings or gore; nothing of Greenbull. (Decisions, "City brief", "City colours")
8. **The alien things** (boulders, the kaiju's meteors): dark rock with glowing cracks, in navy, purple and magenta, kept apart from the city's palette. (Decisions, "Boulders", "City colours")
9. **No real brands, words or characters:** no real logos or badges, no readable real words (signs carry Japanese-like marks that are not words), and no exact copy of an existing character: the kaiju is Godzilla-style, never Godzilla, and never named. (Decisions, "Real-world references", "City brief")
10. **The subjects keep their look:** the car is a 1967 Mustang GT fastback in Greenbull's dark green with two centred white stripes and a gap between them; the minions are light-green four-legged lizards, being redesigned as car-sized mini kaiju with a toothed snapping jaw (Decisions, "The minion, redesigned"); the kaiju is a giant Godzilla-style monster; the ground is asphalt with white lane lines, zebra crossings and light cracks; the alert signs are picture-only (red outline, white inside, the kaiju's black silhouette). (Decisions, "The car", "The minion", "The kaiju", "Ground", "City brief")

Greenbull's logo (emblem and wordmark) is flat brand art: exempt from rule 2's shading and detail, but it follows rule 1 (Decisions, "Greenbull's look").

Each wall loses a band of rows under its lit top lip (134 or 138 rows become 96), keeping its ground floor; the small and long buildings, which stood half a unit inside their footprint, are widened to fill it by repeating one unit in the middle of each roof and wall, and lose their pavement; the parapets come out by reading the roof one unit further in. The rooftop props are never cut: the art is built again without them from the PixelLab pieces in `art-archive/T-129/raw/` and `art-archive/T-257/raw/` (the rebuild is checked to equal today's files pixel for pixel), the box is cut from that, and the props' own pixels are put back whole. #### Rev Charge's charging and boost effect

Task T-466 made the art for Rev Charge's effect (Drifting, Decisions, "Driving power-ups") with a free script, `game/tools/build_rev_charge.py`, no PixelLab (0 generations), through the style loop: kept version 1, scored 7/10, below 8 after 3 refines, noted for the board's playtest (the Style Evaluator's notes: the glow's flame reads as a pointed teardrop rather than a small flame). Eleven frames of 64 x 64, drawn pointing right: four charging frames (a heat glow in oranges and yellows, stepped with a dithered outer halo, growing 25, 50, 75, 100 %), two full-charge pulse frames (a hot white core, alternated), and five boost frames (pale blue-grey speed lines that shorten as the boost runs down). The game sheet `game/art/driving/rev_charge/rev_charge.png` (record `rev_charge.json`) turns them to 16 screen directions like the cruise boost's lines; `rev_charge_effect.gd` picks the column by the charge or the boost's time left and the row by the car's heading, drawn at 0.5. The unturned sheet is `rev_charge_base.png` there. Pictures: `art-archive/T-466/screenshots/`.

#### The car without its shadow

Task T-204 made the shadowless sheet (Decisions, "The car without its shadow") with a free script, no PixelLab: `game/art/car/car_iso_noshadow.png` (record `car_iso_noshadow.json`, same size, frames and centre as `car_iso.png`), made by `game/tools/build_car_noshadow.py`. Per frame, a near-black pixel becomes transparent only when it is connected to the transparent background through near-black pixels, lies outside the convex hull of the frame's other car pixels, and is more than one step from them; the thin outline and every other pixel stay as they are, with no new colours. Dark body panels inside that hull (under the sill between the wheels, under the bumpers) keep a little shadow, because it cannot be told from the body there. Used only while the car is in the air (T-205); on the ground the car uses `car_iso.png`. Screenshots of all 16 frames, original next to shadowless: `art-archive/T-204/screenshots/`.

#### Shadows that shrink with height

Task T-454 built the rule in Decisions, "Shadows shrink with height", in code with no new art. Every object in the air draws a dark ground circle, 2:1 on screen, on the surface right under it. That surface is the street, or a rooftop's or ramp's top when the object is over one. The shadow's size depends on the object's height above that surface, not above the street, and every shadow gets it from one shared curve (`game/scripts/driving/shadow_size.gd`). At the surface the shadow is the object's own size. Higher up it is `1 / (1 + height / 4)` of that size, so it is half size at 4 units, and it never gets smaller than 35 % (reached at about 7.4 units). The shadow shrinks fastest just after the object leaves the ground, so small hops still show. The curve and the 35 % floor are the agent's proposals for the playtest. Which objects use it:

- **The car in the air**: its round shadow (`car_shadow.gd`). Full size is the car's width, 1 unit across, the same as before.
- **A falling gift pack**: the same shadow at its landing spot. Full size is the package's width on screen (40 pixels). It grows as the package comes down and goes when the package lands.
- **A falling minion**: a ground circle of its body's size, in the car shadow's colour. It shows only while the minion falls, because on the ground a minion has no shadow (board, 2026-10-15).
- **A falling kaiju**: its own ground shadow stays on the ground under it while it falls and shrinks with height. Before this task it had no shadow in the air.
- **A thrown Molotov bottle**: a small shadow, 0.5 units across at full size, that does not spin with the bottle.

Screenshots: `art-archive/T-454/screenshots/`.

Every pixel is opaque or empty, so there is no blur, bloom or smoothing. The halo and floor glow pulse in steps and a lighter arc travels round the ring; both stop while paused. ## 8. Extended narrative

*Source: [extended-narrative.md](extended-narrative.md). The deeper story context and the game's tone. Most of it is never shown to players, but it puts the game on the rails, justifies future features in the plot, and sets the voice of every user-facing text and graphic.*

The player is Stunt Driver, sent by the sponsor Greenbull to cities hit by humanitarian crises and disasters, just to drift for the cameras. Every run is livestreamed to Greenbull's audience: good driving earns likes, and likes earn gift packs. The tone is satirical and tongue-in-cheek: Greenbull isn't evil, just completely out of touch, and the player should sense that their fun is slightly unethical. Each city is a level with its own monster boss; the first is Crash City and its kaiju.

### Decisions

- This document changes rarely. It puts the game on the rails: it decides what can be developed in future and how the plot justifies it, so it may hold details that only become useful later.
- Agents read it before producing any user-facing text or graphics, together with Visual style for graphics (how tasks enforce this: `tasks/README.md`).
- Overarching plot: humanitarian crises are happening around the world. Greenbull sends the player to each affected city, and each city is a new level.
- Each level's final boss is a different type of monster. The kaiju is the first level's boss, in Crash City.
- The player is **Stunt Driver**, a stunt driver sponsored by the brand **Greenbull**, sent into each disaster just to drift and show off.
- **The rebrand** (board, 2026-10-26): the sponsor, first called Redgull, is renamed **Greenbull**, one word, with a new logo and colours (Visual style, Decisions, "The rebrand"). The texts no longer explain what the brand sells: they just say Greenbull and let the player assume. Its role in the story and its voice don't change.
- **Tone:** satirical, ironic and tongue-in-cheek. It makes fun of soulless corporate language, social media and brand obsession. Greenbull is not evil, just completely out of touch and focused on profit. Playing is fun, but the player should sense that what they are doing is slightly unethical, and the game highlights this whenever it can.
- Greenbull's logo is a **cool bull's head** in dark green, light green and a little yellow (its look and colours: Visual style, Decisions, "Greenbull's look"). The brand looks cool and confident, and that polish is part of the joke: a slick logo on a company that is out of touch.
- Every run is **livestreamed** to Greenbull's audience. Driving earns **likes**: in the MVP, drifting (challenges are left out of the MVP; Level design, Decisions).
- **Likes are XP.** Players only ever see "likes", never "XP"; the board and the agents may say XP internally. Each level threshold is a likes threshold, and filling the likes bar earns a **gift pack**: the weapon reward on level-up. (2026-10-08) Greenbull delivers each gift pack by helicopter, dropping it into the disaster for Stunt Driver to drive over (how it plays: Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Gift pack drop"; board, 2026-10-16).
- **Greenbull funds the car's upgrades** between runs, all in service of the sponsorship.
- Weapon names, the level-up wording, descriptions and other user-facing text are written by the Narrative Theme Agent, using this document to get the tone; the board doesn't define them. That agent also chooses how likes are shown (the word, a heart icon, or both).
- The first map is downtown Tokyo under attack from the kaiju, the final boss: a giant monster in the style of Godzilla that is not called Godzilla. Its name is still to come from the board; until then it is "the kaiju". The city has put up a few alert banners about it.
- The city's people are not shown for now: only the signs they put up (the alert banners, picture-only).
- **Subs** (board, 2026-10-28): the stream's audience shows in two ways. **Live viewers** are the hype of the moment (the combo, rising with tricks and crashing with crashes). **Subs** are what the stream builds up: drifting brings them, and every full **sub goal** gets Greenbull to send a gift pack. "Subs" replaces "likes" in every player-facing text, and in Text rules, rule 2 (the vocabulary). (T-331)

### Content

#### Text rules

The text style guide: every piece of player-facing text is checked against these rules, each written once here (with Visual style's Rules, the style guide the style loop scores against; `tasks/README.md`, "The style loop"). Each rule condenses a decision; when the decision changes, its rule changes with it. Rules marked *(script)* are checked by a script, the others by the Style Evaluator.

1. **Tone:** satirical, ironic and tongue-in-cheek. It makes fun of soulless corporate language, social media and brand obsession. Greenbull is out of touch and focused on profit, never evil and never sincere; the fun should feel slightly unethical. The city's people and their fear are never the joke. No grimdark, gore or earnest heroics. (Decisions, "Tone"; Content, "The alert banners")
2. **Vocabulary** *(script, banned words)*: the player sees "subs" for what they earn toward a gift pack and "live viewers" for the audience counter, never "likes", "XP" or "points", and no "Hype Lv" or hype level (board, 2026-10-28); the weapon reward is a "gift pack"; the player is "Stunt Driver"; the sponsor is "Greenbull", never "Redgull" (its old name); the run is a livestream to Greenbull's audience; the monster is "the kaiju", never "Godzilla" and never given a name. (Decisions)
3. **Who speaks:** Greenbull's voice is for Greenbull's things (gift packs, level-up, garage, the stream). The city never speaks in Greenbull's voice: its signs are picture-only. No line takes the form "Greenbull says ..." (HUD and menus, Decisions, "No "Greenbull says ..." lines"). No real brands. (Decisions; Visual style, Decisions, "City brief")
4. **Format and length, by kind of text** *(script)*:
   - **Trick and combo popups:** one short line in capitals ending in "!", like LONG DRIFT!, AIR 360! and COMBO BROKEN! (HUD and menus, Content, "Trick popups", "Combo broken popup")
   - **Level-up cards:** a title of at most 30 characters and a description of at most 90 that says first what the card does, then at most one satirical aside. (T-051, T-171)
   - **Garage upgrades:** a name of at most 25 characters and a description of at most 80 that names no number. (T-268)
   - **Menu and settings labels:** short and plain, in sentence case, like "Music volume". (HUD and menus, Content)

#### The first map: downtown Tokyo under attack

The first level is downtown Tokyo at night, in the middle of the kaiju's attack (Decisions, 2026-10-14). The kaiju is a giant monster in the style of Godzilla, never called Godzilla, and still unnamed: until the board names it, the story and every text call it "the kaiju". It is the level's final boss, and the whole city is already reacting to it.

What the player drives through is a living, frightened city, not an empty set. The skyscrapers are still lit, their towers rising out of view, so the car feels small beside them. Shorter buildings show their roofs. Pavements run around every building. The streets show light cracks from the disaster (Visual style, Decisions). Neon signs are still on, with Japanese-like marks that are not real words (Visual style, Decisions), as the city's own night look. Nothing here belongs to Greenbull: the city has nothing to do with the brand, and Greenbull's colours and branding stay off the buildings, banners and pavements.

How it fits the story: Greenbull has sent Stunt Driver to a city that is in the middle of a disaster, only to drift for the cameras and for the livestream's likes. The contrast is the joke and the unease: people are in danger, and the run is entertainment. The city's own signs are what is left of the people's voice in that scene. Greenbull never writes them.

#### The alert banners

A few alert banners about the kaiju hang on buildings or stand as signs on the pavement (Decisions, 2026-10-14). The people of the city put them up, the way a city warns itself in an emergency: quickly, by hand or by the city, to tell everyone that the monster is near. They are not Greenbull's banners and carry none of its look.

Their purpose in the story is to tell the player, without any dialogue, that this city knows what is coming and is afraid of it, and to give the player a first look at the kaiju before it appears. Their look is a silly, minimalistic pixel painting of the kaiju's head or of its general Godzilla-like body shape, as if drawn by someone in a hurry. The silliness is the tone: the warning is earnest, the drawing is goofy, and the contrast sits close to the game's satire without making fun of the people. They are few, so each one is noticed.

#### Looking after consistency

All the city's generated art (the tall skyscraper bases, the shorter buildings with roofs, the pavements and the banners) follows one brief so it matches: night, dark navy and purple base, pink and cyan neon drawn into the sprites, Japanese-like marks and no real words, a damage level for the attack (the board approves it), no Greenbull colours or branding. The brief itself is given to the art tasks by the Narrative Theme Agent (task T-128); the parts the board approves are kept in Visual style, Decisions.

### References

- Final GDD (historical; superseded by the game area docs): [short-gdd/Solid_Carbide_-_Final_GDD.pdf](short-gdd/Solid_Carbide_-_Final_GDD.pdf), section "Narrative Theme".


## 9. HUD and menus

*Source: [hud-and-menus.md](hud-and-menus.md). What the player sees on screen during a run (the HUD) and the menus around it: pause, level-up and their look. Which screens exist and how they connect is in Game loop architecture.*

During a run the HUD shows the car's HP, a timer counting down from 8:00, the XP bar and level, the coins collected, and the kaiju's health once it appears. Levelling up pauses the game and shows the weapon choice as simple cards. Escape pauses the game, and the pause screen has a camera zoom slider. In the MVP every screen is kept plain; their visual style comes after the MVP.

### Decisions

- During a run, the HUD shows: the car's HP as a bar; the run timer, counting down from 8:00; the XP bar, shown to the player as a likes bar (Extended narrative, Decisions), and the current level; the coins collected this run; and the kaiju's health once it appears, as a bar above the kaiju (see below).
- When the player levels up and then drives over the dropped gift pack (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Gift pack drop"; board, 2026-10-16), the game pauses and the level-up screen shows the options (what is offered: Weapons, Decisions). Each option has a title and a description. In the MVP it is kept simple: cards, clicked to take one (first a button on each card, 2026-10-08; clicked directly since 2026-10-31). 
- The level-up screen's cards take the game's comic look, like the trick popups and the combo counter: white rounded cards with black borders and the Bangers font, over the dimmed, paused run. The player picks a card with the keyboard (A/D or the arrow keys move between the cards, Enter or Space takes the highlighted one) or by clicking the card itself (Decisions, "Gift menu cards are clicked directly", 2026-10-31).
- The HUD shows the current combo multiplier as a counter next to the likes bar. When the player completes a trick, a short comic-style text pops out from the car with the trick's name and what it added to the multiplier (combo: Game loop architecture, Decisions). Extended-drift popups are smaller than the others, since they come every second.
- After the MVP, if challenges come back (2026-10-11): when the player completes a challenge, the likes it gave pop out from the car the same way, not on the HUD (the score flash in Game loop architecture, Decisions).
- The UI Agent proposes a first layout for where each HUD element goes on screen, and the board adjusts it in playtest.
- The car's health bar stands upright at the top left, filling from the bottom up, with its label above it. The likes bar is horizontal, centred at the bottom of the screen, with the heart, "Likes" and the level in one row above it and the combo counter above that. Labels line up with the bar they belong to.
- The combo counter is hidden when there is no combo (multiplier x1.0) and shows as soon as a trick raises it.
- **A bigger health bar with the heart, and the weapons beside it** (board, 2026-10-22): the car's health bar at the top left stays upright but becomes 3 times wider and twice as tall (from 24 x 160 to 72 x 320 pixels); its "Car Health" label goes, and the likes bar's red heart (the same one, board-approved red) sits under it. To its right, a column of small square icons shows each weapon the car has taken from gift packs this run, one per weapon, with "x2", "x3" ... when it has been taken more than once (its tier), in the HUD's comic font like the combo counter. (T-276)
- **A thicker likes bar that springs** (board, 2026-10-22): the likes bar at the bottom is 4 times thicker (from 16 to 64 pixels tall, still half the screen wide), and when likes come in it shoots quickly up to its new fill, overshoots a little and settles, instead of jumping there at once. The texts above it, the burning bar at x4 and the level-up animation follow the new size. (T-273)
- **No "Greenbull says ..." lines** (board, 2026-10-22; Redgull renamed Greenbull, 2026-10-26): the board dislikes text in the form "Greenbull says X" (first "Redgull says X") (two level-up card descriptions used it: the flamethrower's tier 6 and the underglow's tier 2). They are rewritten without it, and no new text uses that form. (T-268)
- **Airtime counter** (board, 2026-10-21): while the car is airborne, a small label near the bottom right of where the combo popups show counts its airtime up as a plain number with two decimals (0.00, 0.01 ... in seconds, no unit), next to a small icon standing for a jump (a wing or similar). It disappears on landing, when the airtime trick pays out (Drifting, Decisions, "Airtime trick"). Placeholder icon until it has art. Built in T-243 as a proposal: white Bangers number with a black outline and a code-drawn white wing, right of the screen's centre and a little below it (`game/docs/hud-and-menus/hud.md`, "Airtime counter (HUD)").
- **Drift counter** (board, 2026-10-22): while the car is drifting, a second small label next to the airtime counter counts the drift's length up the same way (0.00, seconds, no unit), with its own small icon standing for a drift; it disappears when the drift ends and pays out. Placeholder icon until it has art. Built in T-247 as a proposal: the airtime counter's look with an icon of two skid marks, directly under the airtime counter (`game/docs/hud-and-menus/hud.md`, "Drift counter (HUD)"). Since there is no drifting in the air, the drift counter ends as the car leaves an edge, so the two show together only for a moment, if at all.
- **Combo broken popup** (board, 2026-10-21): when a crash cuts the combo (hitting a wall, a building, a boulder or taking damage, Game loop architecture, Decisions), a popup like the trick popups pops from the car, but in red and in a broken, cracked style. Only on a crash, not when the combo drains away. The red is a warning red. Its text: HUD and menus, Content (T-244). (T-245)
- The combo heats up in three steps as it climbs: the counter changes look at x2, changes more at x3, and from x4 up (the top step, even though the combo goes on to its cap) it is fully maxed out, with the likes bar looking like it is on fire. When the combo drops, the look drops with it. The combo counter and the "Hype Lv" text take the game's comic look (the Bangers font of the trick popups, hard pixel edges). The fire is drawn in code first (no PixelLab), in oranges and yellows, never in Greenbull's colours; generated art only if the board finds it weak in playtest. No sound for now.
- The trick popups heat up with the combo in the same steps: unchanged black and white below x2, a hot orange or yellow accent at x2, a stronger one at x3, and a flaming edge from x4. The letters stay readable on white. Popups are always drawn above the buildings, so a building never hides one.
- The heart next to "Likes" matches the HUD's comic look: a flat red heart with a thick dark outline (first Redgull red; it stays red after the rebrand, as a social-media heart: Visual style, Decisions, "Red after the rebrand") like the text's, sized to the "LIKES" text. Drawn by script, no PixelLab.
- The trick popups look like real comic book popups: a white burst bubble with a black border and black lettering in a heavy, slanted comic font (Bangers), on one straight baseline.
- The trick popups are white rounded rectangles (not jagged bursts), with the black border and black lettering.
- Trick popups stay with the car: each one follows the car for its whole life (popping above it, rising and fading relative to it), so it stays readable at drift speed.
- The main menu shows the title "SOLID CARBIDE" in big letters, with a discreet "(work in progress)" underneath.
- Escape pauses the game. In the MVP the pause screen says "Paused", with a hint that Escape resumes, and has one setting: the camera zoom slider, labelled "Camera zoom level", which zooms the view behind the screen live while the game stays paused (Drifting, Decisions). The screen is a compact dark strip, only as tall as its content, placed just below the HUD timer so the two never overlap and as much of the map as possible stays visible (board, 2026-10-11). A full pause menu, with more settings, comes in the final release.
- The pause screen also has two checkboxes under the zoom slider, "Camera smoothing" and "Dynamic camera" (the board's names; what they do: Drifting, Decisions), and, while the dynamic camera is on, two temporary tuning buttons, "Set min zoom" and "Set max zoom", with the stored values shown next to them. The buttons are removed once the board has settled the values.
- The pause screen has an **"SFX volume"** slider (the board's name) for the sound effects' volume, from 0 to 100, starting at **0, so sound effects are silent until the player turns them up**. Like the zoom, the player's choice is saved between sessions. Music, when it comes, is separate.
- The pause screen also has a **music volume** slider (board, 2026-10-20), under the SFX volume slider and laid out like it, from 0 to 100, saved between sessions like the others. Its label comes from the Narrative Theme Agent (T-208); its starting value is a proposal for the playtest (T-210). What the music is: Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Music".
- Settings exposed for playtests and development (for example the flamethrower from the start, the kaiju's early arrival) go under an internal dev flag: players never see them.
- The kaiju's health bar sits on top of the kaiju in the world and follows it, instead of in a corner of the HUD: about as wide as the kaiju (it follows the kaiju's width, so it still fits the final art), neon purple on a white background with a black outline and thin black dividers at every 10% of its health, in a subtle version of the combo popups' comic style. No label. It is always drawn above buildings, so it shows even when the kaiju is behind one.
- The level-up screen's weapon cards each show an image of the weapon.
- The level-up screen's header title is lettered in cream (RGB 246, 250, 232) with a dark outline (RGB 14, 22, 18, 4 pixels), to read on a dark green ribbon; the card titles, descriptions and buttons keep black ink on the cream cards. (T-310)
- Level-ups are animated: the likes bar plays a short animation when the player levels up, and the level-up screen animates in. The level-up screen gets art themed on the sponsor, since the weapons it offers arrive as its gift packs; its animation uses that art. First red and gold for Redgull (board, 2026-10-15); after the rebrand, Greenbull's dark green leading, with light green and a little yellow (board, 2026-10-26; Visual style, Decisions, "Greenbull's look").
- **Restart and Exit on the pause screen** (board, 2026-10-28): the pause screen gets two buttons, **"Restart"** and **"Exit"** (the board's names): Restart ends the run and starts a fresh one straight away; Exit ends the run and goes back to the main menu (Exit on the main menu still closes the game). Where they sit, whether they ask "are you sure?" first, and what happens to the run's coins are the agents' proposals for the playtest. (T-327)
- **The HUD looks like a livestream** (board, 2026-10-28): the board places the pieces on its HUD layout page (https://claude.ai/artifact/CSHYCDV9xZbSYwQGUt5SJ4), and the game follows the positions saved there. The pieces: the **timer** at the bottom left as a digital pixel-art clock whose digits start green and turn yellow, orange and red as the time nears 0:00 (the switch points are a proposal); the **live viewers counter** at the bottom right, in place of the combo counter (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "The combo shows as live viewers"); the **sub goal** at the bottom centre, in place of the likes bar and its "Likes ... Hype Lv" row: a black square that fills green from the bottom as subs come in, with the gift pack inside it greyed out until the goal is reached, when it lights up, and the subs count under it as "{subs} / {goal}" with a subs icon; the **hearts** in a row at the top left, in place of the upright health bar (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "Hearts instead of health points"). The art is generated with PixelLab (the board: "don't be stingy"). (T-331 to T-339)
- **Tricks bring viewers, shown in one colour** (board, 2026-10-28): the live viewers counter has its own colour, used for nothing else. A trick popup keeps its name as today, and its amount shows as the viewers it brought ("+12K" with an eye icon) in that colour; that amount then flies across the screen into the counter, which bumps when it arrives. When a crash breaks the combo, the counter flashes red and a "-{viewers}" drops away from it as the number falls. (T-336)
- **"Hype Lv" is gone** (board, 2026-10-28): the level is shown only by the sub goal square (it fills, the gift lights up, the level-up goes on); there is no "Hype Lv" text and no level-up pop on it, and none of its code is kept (T-337). The older passages above that mention it describe the game before this change. The board also confirmed the proposals for the live viewers: 2,500 viewers at x1, the heat steps at 20K, 85K and 236K, and fire only from 1M (T-332, T-336), and the PixelLab cap of 40 for the HUD art (T-339). The weapon icons column may be taller than the old health bar did: the health bar is gone, replaced by the hearts, so it doesn't matter (T-338). The coins counter moves to the bottom left above the clock (T-341).
- **Reactions like a livestream** (board, 2026-10-28): little reaction icons (likes, thumbs up, hearts and the like) **burst out of the sub goal square** when the goal is reached and the gift pack comes, and **float up from the bottom of the screen** now and then, at uneven gaps like a real stream, when the live viewers count is high (more often at each heat step). They are small and partly transparent, kept to the edges and bottom of the screen, never over the car and under the HUD pieces, so they don't hide the road. The rates and the cap on how many show at once are proposals for the playtest. Placeholder icons first; the art comes after. (T-351, T-352)
- **Bad reactions when the combo breaks** (board, 2026-10-29): when a crash cuts the combo (the COMBO BROKEN! moment), the stream reacts badly: a burst of bad reactions rises from the live viewers counter, on the same right-side lane as the floating reactions. Six of them: a crying-laughing face, a thumbs down (a dislike) and a face peeking between its hands (the board's), and a broken heart, a skull and a screaming face (the board left the last three to the Project Lead). The count, spread and speed are proposals for the playtest. Placeholders first; the art is drawn by script like T-352's icons. The board also said the livestream HUD's art needs no rework (the viewers fire, the subs icon and the heart stay as they are), and no ticket to move the pause strip up. (T-356, T-357)
- **The runs list** (board, 2026-10-29): the main menu gets a new button that opens a list of the player's past runs, each with the stats from its recap screen, saved on this computer. What each row shows, and whether a row opens that run's full recap, are proposals for the playtest. The recap screen closes with a Continue button or an X at the top right (Game loop architecture, Decisions, "The recap always closes a run"). (T-362, T-364) **Deferred to the final release** (board, 2026-10-29, the MVP cut).
- **The last MVP round: no new scope after it** (board, 2026-10-29): the tutorial slides, the trick list and turning the sound effects off (the three entries below) are the last features for the MVP. After them the board adds no new scope until the MVP is done, apart from polish tickets. Built as one goal: the board's go to build the text, the slides and the art back to back and review them all in one playtest at the end, with a PixelLab cap of 40 for the trick illustrations.
- **Tutorial slides before the first run** (board, 2026-10-29): when the player presses Start, before the run begins (the clock and everything), the game shows **three slides**. A right arrow and a left arrow move between them; the last slide has a **Start** button (not an X) that starts the run, and a **"Don't show again"** checkbox: if it is ticked when the player presses Start, the slides don't appear on later Starts (saved on this computer). Where the checkbox sits (on the last slide, a proposal) is the agents' proposal. **Slide 1, the controls:** W, A, S and D and what each does, and that accelerating while turning drifts the car on its own. **Slide 2, the loop:** the list of tricks the game counts (drift, 360, alternate drift, air 180, air 360, airtime, thread the needle), each with a small **still pixel art illustration** of the car's movement for that trick (a path arrow, for example a loop for the 360, an S for the alternate drift, a jump arc for the air tricks); then that tricks bring more viewers, viewers bring subs, and at each sub goal a gift pack arrives with a weapon that helps the player survive and keep the enemies away. **Slide 3, the goal:** chain as many tricks as possible to get the most weapons, to be at your strongest when the kaiju arrives with 1 minute left (7:00 into the 8:00 run). The illustrations: made both with PixelLab (cap 40 generations for the set) and drawn by script, and QA compares which reads better; the better one goes in. The text is a text ticket's, in the game's voice.
- **A trick list in the pause screen** (board, 2026-10-29): the pause screen (the game's settings) gets a **trick list** button that opens a sub-panel showing the same trick list as slide 2 (the tricks with their illustrations only, without the rest of slide 2), with a way back to the pause screen.
- **No sound effects in the MVP** (board, 2026-10-29): every sound effect is off for the MVP and the sound effects slider is hidden from the pause screen (done in T-389: the row is hidden while the switch is off, and the layout closes the gap); the music stays, with its slider. The sound effect code stays in the game for later.
- **MVP nice-to-haves, only after the last round** (board, 2026-10-29): inside the MVP's scope, but started only once the tutorial slides and the sound effects change are done: the main menu polish, a consistent HUD, a HUD size slider with a HUD that scales with the window, bigger minions and the minions stuck on ramps (Enemies). The board may still add one or two weapons; otherwise only polish after this.
- **Main menu polish** (board, 2026-10-29): the title "SOLID CARBIDE" in a pixel-art font, the "(work in progress)" line kept and styled to match, and behind the menu a **splash cover**, an AI-generated pixel art image (Visual style, Decisions, "The splash cover").
- **A consistent HUD** (board, 2026-10-29): today's HUD pieces look as if they came from different games; they get one visual language (outline, colours, fonts, panel shapes) so they read as one interface.
- **The HUD scales with the window, and a HUD size slider** (board, 2026-10-29): the HUD keeps a predictable place and a sensible size at any window size and resolution, ultrawide included (today it stays the same pixel size, so it looks tiny on a big or ultrawide screen). The pause screen gets a slider that sets the HUD's size, saved on this computer.
- **Bigger gift pack arrows in the gift box's colours** (board, 2026-10-31): the arrows that point to gift packs off screen are 3 times as big as today's (30 by 24 pixels at the HUD's base size), and wear the gift box's colours (Visual style, Decisions, "The gift pack package in Greenbull's colours": Greenbull's dark green box with its light green ribbon) instead of the placeholder pale cyan. As they belong to the gift pack, Greenbull's colours are allowed on them (Visual style, Content, "Rules", rule 6). They keep the HUD's dark outline and stay clear of the HUD parts as today. The build (T-442): 90 by 72 pixels at the HUD's base size, scaled with the HUD's size like the rest of it (the track, the gaps and the outline too); the dark green fills the arrow, the light green is an inner stripe along it (the split is the agents' proposal for the playtest), inside the HUD's dark outline (8, 8, 15). (T-442)
- **One button style across the game** (board, 2026-10-31): every button the player meets (main menu, garage, tutorial slides, level-up screen, pause screen and the end-of-run recap) shares one look and one feel that match the game: the same shape, art, font, colours and outline from the HUD style sheet (Visual style, Content), and the same behaviour when hovered, selected with the keyboard, pressed and disabled. The board's own tools (the level creator and the tuning panel) keep their look. The exact look and feel are the agents' proposals for the board's playtest. (T-446, T-447)
- **The player can move the HUD's pieces** (board, 2026-10-31): from the in-game settings (the pause screen), the player can edit the HUD's placement: drag each HUD piece to where they want it, reset the layout to the default, and keep it, saved on this computer like the other settings. Which pieces can move, how they snap and the controls are the agents' proposals for the playtest. (T-452, T-453)
- **Gift menu cards are clicked directly** (board, 2026-10-31): every gift menu (the level-up gift pack's weapon choices and the driving power-up overlay) has no Take it button on its cards: the whole card is clicked to take it, and it shows it can be, reacting to hover and to keyboard selection; the keyboard keeps working as before. (T-474, T-475)
- **The board passes through every menu and text before the MVP** (board, 2026-11-01): before the MVP release the board reviews every screen the player can meet and every piece of player-facing text, item by item. A script builds the material for it: a screenshot of every screen and a list of every text, rebuilt after each change.
- **The tutorial slides are redrawn, with clips of the real car** (board, 2026-11-01, from the Project Lead's draft page): four slides instead of three. **1, Drive:** the W, A, S, D keys as labelled keycaps and the rule "W + turn = drift", beside a clip of the car drifting seen from higher up and zoomed out, so the drift's path shows from where it starts; no flavour line and no "no drift button" label. **2, Tricks bring gifts:** the loop as a chain of four steps with the HUD's own icons (a trick, the viewer count, the sub goal, the gift pack with its weapons), and under it three clips: a long drift, an alt drift, and the car taking a ramp at speed and flying, gaining hang time while it spins (an air 180 or 360) in one clip. **3, Missions:** the notebook page and the four driving power-ups. **4, Survive the stream:** the 8-minute run as a timeline with gift packs along it and the kaiju in the last minute, then Go live and "Don't show again"; no hearts and no sentence. The clips are recorded from the game itself, on a simple background. Every slide has a Skip control that jumps to the last slide (the board approved the draft with it, 2026-11-01). Its lines come from the Narrative Theme Agent.
- **Arrow keys in the main menu and the garage** (board, 2026-11-02, after playing the itch.io build): the main menu and the garage can be used with the arrow keys alone: the arrows move the keyboard selection between the buttons (and the garage's upgrades), Enter or Space presses the selected one, and the selection always shows (the shared button's focus plate). The mouse works as before. **W, A, S and D work the same as the arrow keys** (board, 2026-11-02, swipe-deck review of T-492: W up, S down, A left, D right).
- **Every screen scales with the window** (board, 2026-11-02, after playing the itch.io build): the gift pack (level-up) screen and the pause screen (the settings) look very small on big resolutions, and so may others. Every screen and menu the player meets scales with the window by the HUD's rule (Content, "The HUD scales with the window"), so it covers the same share of the screen at any resolution; this replaces that section's "keep their size" for the screens. A game-wide scan at several resolutions finds every piece that does not scale, and each is fixed. Things drawn in the world at the camera's zoom (trick popups, the kaiju's health bar) are not screens and keep following the camera.
- **Each trick shows the keys that make it** (board, 2026-11-01, from the Project Lead's draft page "Trick Controls Draft"): the trick list in the pause screen shows, for every trick, a **keycap recipe**: the keys held together joined with +, the steps joined with an arrow, and a short note under each step (for example W + A/D, hold 1 s or more, then let go); a key marked "/D" means either turn key works. Each trick in the trick list also has a **clip of the real car** doing it, with a small **live W A S D pad** in the clip's corner that lights each key exactly when the recording pressed it. **Thread the needle shows no keys** (the player just drives through the gap): its row has its clip and its rule only. On **tutorial slide 2** the three clips get the same live key pad; the slide adds no other tricks or recipes, so it stays uncluttered. Clips are recorded for the tricks that have none yet (FULL 360!, AIR 360!, THREAD THE NEEDLE!, and HANG TIME! without a spin). The board approved merging this straight after QA, without its own playtest of each ticket (2026-11-01).

### Content

#### The HUD's style in code (T-429, goal G-008; proposals for the playtest)

The HUD pieces follow the HUD style sheet (Visual style, Decisions, "The HUD style sheet"); the values sit in `hud_style.gd` (`game/docs/hud-and-menus/hud.md`). Words are Bangers with the near-black outline (8, 8, 15): outline 6 on the coins, the sub goal, "WATCHING" and the flight and drop numbers; 8 on the big numbers (weapon counts, airtime and drift counters, the viewers number, the combo heat steps). The trick and combo broken popups use that near-black for letters and borders, the kaiju bar for its outline and dividers (2 px). The pause strip's title and text are Bangers, shown in capitals (the text itself is unchanged; its three slider numbers stay in the default font, since Bangers would make the strip 10 pixels shorter); the level-up title has outline 6. The **clock** is T-339's art: the steel panel at 2x (exactly its 200 x 72) and the drawn seven-segment digits at 2x, tinted with the time step's colour over a dim unlit 8 (the step colour at 22%, a proposal); no system font is left in the HUD. The **weapon icons** are their own 24 x 24 art (T-429, script-drawn from the card pictures, 0 PixelLab; it scored 7 of 10 in the style loop, kept for the playtest) shown at 2x in the same 48 pixel slot, so every HUD sprite now has the same pixel size.

#### The shared button (T-446; proposals for the playtest)

Every button the player meets is one shared button (Decisions, "One button style across the game"): the main menu's three, the garage's Buy and Back, the tutorial slides' two arrows and Start (and the "Don't show again" checkbox, styled to match), the pause screen's Trick list, Restart, Exit and the trick list's Back (and its two camera checkboxes), and the recap's Continue and X. It is defined once, beside the HUD style sheet's values in `game/scripts/hud/hud_style.gd` (`HudStyle.style_button`, `HudStyle.style_checkbox`); the screens only call it and keep their buttons' text, place, size, keys and actions. The board's tools keep their own look: the level creator, the drift tuning panel and the pause strip's two camera tuning buttons (Set min and max zoom).

- **Plate** (T-447): one 9-slice plate per state in `game/art/ui/` (`button_plate_normal.png`, `_hover`, `_focus`, `_pressed`, `_disabled`; record `button_plates.json`), 72 x 22 art pixels shown at 2x, slice margins 3 art pixels; the plates are drawn in the HUD style sheet's steel (Visual style, Content, "The shared button's plates"). No tint and no recolour in code: every state is its own picture. The level-up screen's own plate (`game/art/level_up/button_plate*.png`) stays as that screen's art but is no longer used by the button.
- **Text:** Bangers in capitals, the sheet's light label colour (235, 242, 255) with its near-black outline 6; size 28, and 16 with outline 4 on the pause strip's small buttons.
- **States and feel:** hovered shows the brighter hover plate and turns the text white; keyboard-selected draws the focus plate, a bright ring with an open middle, over whichever state the button is in, and the text turns white; pressed shows the sunk plate with the text 2 pixels lower (the press-down); disabled shows the dim plate and greys the text (the garage's Buy with too few coins). The mouse pointer becomes a hand over a button. The tutorial arrows are drawn in the text colour with the outline and drop with the press too; the recap's X is white with the outline.
- **Checkbox:** no plate; the same text, the same keyboard ring plate, and a square with a light frame on steel, a light mark when checked.

#### The HUD scales with the window (T-431, goal G-008; proposals for the playtest)

Decisions, 'The HUD scales with the window, and a HUD size slider'. **The scaling rule:** the HUD is laid out on the board's layout page (1152 x 648), and at any window size the whole HUD is drawn at one scale: the smaller of the window's width over 1152 and its height over 648, times the HUD size slider's value in percent. Each piece keeps its corner or edge (hearts and weapon icons top left, coins and clock bottom left, viewers counter bottom right, the sub goal on the right edge at its share of the height) and its margins and size grow and shrink with that scale, so the HUD covers the same share of the screen at any resolution. On a wider screen than 16:9 (the 3440 x 1440 ultrawide) the height decides, and the pieces stay at the far corners; on a narrower one the width decides. Examples at 100: 1 at 1152 x 648, 1.67 at 1920 x 1080, 2.22 at 2560 x 1440 and 3440 x 1440, 0.83 at 960 x 540. The scale is often not a whole number, so the HUD's art is drawn with hard pixel edges (nearest filtering) instead; some art pixels are then one screen pixel wider than others, which the playtest judges. The world camera's zoom is never changed by the HUD. When the HUD size is above 100 the sub goal square moves up just enough to stay 16 layout pixels above the live viewers counter, so they never overlap.

**HUD size slider:** on the pause screen (below, "Pause screen"), from **50 to 125**, in steps of 5, **default 100** (the size the board laid the HUD out at, in proportion to the window). Above 125, all five weapons' icon column would reach the coins counter, since the layout page is already full at 100. Moving it resizes the HUD at once behind the pause strip; it is saved on this computer when the drag ends (and when the pause screen closes) and used at the next start. **Which screens it covers:** the run's HUD only (hearts, weapon icons, coins, clock, sub goal, live viewers counter, reaction icons, the airtime and drift counters and the viewers flying into the counter). The slider changes the HUD only: the screens below scale with the window but not with the slider, and the trick popups and the kaiju's health bar (drawn in the world, at the camera's zoom) keep their size. How it is built: `game/docs/hud-and-menus/hud.md`, "The HUD scales with the window", and `pause-screen.md`.

**The screens scale too (T-494)** (Decisions, "Every screen scales with the window"): every screen and menu uses the same rule as the HUD, through one shared helper (`UiScale`, `game/scripts/ui/ui_scale.gd`, which the HUD's scale also comes from). Each screen is laid out at 1152 x 648 and drawn at the smaller of the window's width over 1152 and its height over 648, so it covers the same share of the window at every 16:9 size (1280 x 720 to 3840 x 2160) and keeps its shape; on an ultrawide window it keeps its height share and the extra width is left and right, like the HUD. Screens it covers: the main menu, the pause screen with its trick list and HUD layout editor, the level-up (gift pack) screen, the driving power-up overlay and the recap. The garage and the tutorial slides already scaled to fit the window and now use the same helper for it; the time's up card keeps its own whole-number scale. Pixel art and text are drawn with nearest filtering, so they stay hard-edged (the text is the 1152 x 648 text enlarged, blocky rather than blurred). Keyboard and mouse work as before at every size. How it is built: `game/docs/hud-and-menus/hud.md`, "Every screen scales with the window".

#### The HUD layout editor (T-453; proposals for the playtest)

Decisions, "The player can move the HUD's pieces". **Opening it:** the pause screen has an "Edit HUD layout" button (the shared button, T-446, small) in the row of buttons at the bottom of the strip, after "Trick list" (its own row would have made the strip taller than half the screen); it shows only in a run (the drift prototype has no HUD). Pressing it hides the pause strip and its dim, so the HUD shows as it is behind the paused run, and draws a thin white frame round each piece that can move. A small dark bar in the middle of the screen holds the hint "Drag a piece to move it.", "Reset layout" and "Done" (T-452's texts, in `game/data/pause_text.json`). **Which pieces move:** the hearts row, the weapon icons column, the coins counter, the timer clock, the sub goal (its square, flames and subs label together) and the live viewers counter. The airtime and drift counters (shown only in the air or in a drift, next to the car), the reaction icons and the trick popups stay where they are. **Controls:** press the left mouse button on a piece and drag it; the piece under the pointer lights up a little, the dragged one a little more. Escape works as Done. **Snapping:** a piece snaps to a 4 pixel grid of the layout page and, when it comes within 12 pixels of an edge, to the HUD's usual 16 pixel margin from that edge; it can never leave the screen, even partly. Pieces may overlap if the player puts them on top of each other. **Reset layout** puts every piece back at its default place at once; **Done** saves the layout and returns to the pause screen. **How a place is kept:** each moved piece remembers the corner, edge or centre nearest to it (by the third of the screen its centre is in) and its distance from that point in layout pixels, so a piece left at the bottom right keeps its margins to that corner and a piece left at the top centre stays centred, at any window size and with the HUD size slider (Content, "The HUD scales with the window"); a piece that would leave the screen (a smaller window, a bigger HUD, a row of hearts that grows) is moved back just enough to stay fully on screen.
